title: Referential Integrity
description: Reason about valid references across a database state, distinguish permitted absence from dangling values, and retain an original orphan-detection exercise with stronger fixtures.
notes:
## Valid references depend on the database state

Referential integrity is the rule that a declared reference must satisfy its defined relationship to an allowed parent key. A campus enrollment can name a student through student_id. For a required nonmissing reference, the appropriate student identity must exist in the parent relation. This connects the validity of one fact to another rather than treating every table as an independent collection.

The rule concerns the actual combined state. A child column can contain a type-compatible positive integer while still naming no existing parent. Local range rules do not establish parent existence. Conversely, a parent can exist even when its descriptive name is absent or repeated. A reliable check follows the identifying attributes defined by the relationship instead of guessing from convenient labels.

## The concept and the SQL mechanism differ

Referential integrity describes the intended invariant. A supported, enforced FOREIGN KEY is an SQL mechanism for protecting that invariant. A column ending in _id, a line in a diagram, or a client lookup can communicate intent without enforcing the same rule for every accepted write. Inspect the actual declaration and engine behaviour before describing a database relationship as protected.

A simplified teaching fixture may intentionally omit foreign keys so invalid proposals can be loaded and diagnosed. That is useful for studying audit queries, but it is not evidence that an actual foreign key rejected an invalid insert. State whether the exercise demonstrates reference meaning, diagnosis of a current dataset, or enforcement at the trusted write boundary. These are complementary forms of evidence with different limits.

## Optional absence can be a valid state

A single-column optional department reference can be NULL when the employee is unassigned. If nullability and all other rules permit that absence, it is not a dangling ordinary identifier. A non-NULL value of ninety-nine with no department ninety-nine is a different situation: it asserts a reference that has no allowed parent under the defined mapping.

An orphan audit should distinguish these cases. Requiring a nonmissing child reference before reporting an unmatched parent avoids treating legitimate unassigned employees as violations. If the business relationship is mandatory, the absence is invalid through its required-value policy as well. Keep the two diagnostics clear instead of using one unexplained missing-parent label for every blank or unmatched field.

## Composite relationships need their actual definition

A parent identity can use several attributes, such as campus_code and local_number. A child reference must identify the intended combined parent rather than independently matching one campus and an unrelated number. Type compatibility, supported referenced keys, attribute correspondence, and engine-specific missing-component rules all matter to the legal declaration and resulting accepted states.

An all-or-none optional composite reference can require additional policy beyond a simple single-column analogy. Do not assert that every partially missing reference is always valid or always rejected across products. State the actual supported definition and intended absence contract, then test it on the target engine when possible. This keeps an introductory explanation accurate without pretending one short rule covers every composite edge case.

## Child changes can introduce dangling references

An invalid reference can arrive through an INSERT or through an UPDATE that changes a valid child to an absent parent identity. Both paths should be considered when testing enforcement. A write accepted under proper constraints must preserve the applicable invariant. A preceding screen lookup alone can be insufficient if another operation changes the parent before the later write.

Reference validity also does not mean the choice is semantically correct. An employee can refer to an existing department while actually belonging to another one. A valid student-course reference can still be unauthorized or incorrect for the requested registration. Additional business validation and access checks decide those questions. Existence is an important guarantee, but it is narrower than complete domain truth or authority.

## Parent changes need coordinated consequences

A parent deletion or identity update can invalidate existing child references unless the relationship supplies a compatible action. An enforced definition can restrict the change or apply a deliberately configured supported referential action. A cascade can change or remove related facts; setting an optional reference to NULL can detach it. Those choices have different meanings for ownership and history.

A course being retired from new enrollment does not necessarily justify deleting its historical enrollments. The intended product behaviour may use a status change while preserving parent and child identities. Referential integrity helps make invalid transitions visible, but it does not choose the retention policy automatically. Review the actual lifecycle before treating automatic cascading as the standard answer for every dependency.

## Audit with a preserving join

A LEFT JOIN from proposed children to parents keeps each child even when it has no match. The unmatched parent attributes are NULL in the result. Testing a parent identity that cannot be NULL for a matched row lets the query detect absent parents reliably. Testing an optional parent description instead could incorrectly flag a real parent whose description is unrecorded.

```sql
SELECT e.id, e.name, e.department_id
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.department_id
WHERE e.department_id IS NOT NULL
  AND d.id IS NULL
ORDER BY e.id;
```

The child absence condition follows the optional-reference policy. Existing seed examples with only nonmissing references preserve their expected output under this correction. Adding a fixture with an unassigned employee makes the distinction observable and protects the exercise from teaching that every unmatched join row is automatically an invalid foreign reference.

## Existence tests offer another formulation

A correlated NOT EXISTS condition can ask whether a nonmissing child identifier has no allowed parent. It avoids projecting parent labels and expresses the existence question directly. The child population and absence policy still need the same care. Changing the syntax does not fix a wrong scope condition, incomplete composite identity, or mistaken interpretation of NULL.

For a grouped audit, first define which child rows are invalid, then count them at the requested reporting grain. Counting unmatched child references by proposed department_id can show how many proposals need each missing parent. It does not mean those parents should automatically be created. A correction workflow must distinguish typos, retired codes, wrong scopes, and genuinely new entities under the authorized domain process.

## Other duplicate problems remain independent

A child can have a valid parent reference while violating a separate email uniqueness policy. An employee can have a unique primary identity while pointing to an absent department. One successful integrity check therefore does not imply every rule passed. When an exercise focuses on reference existence, do not filter by unrelated uniqueness assumptions that would hide a relevant child fact.

The retained employee fixture intentionally includes duplicate emails and invalid department-style references so different audits can ask different questions over the same data. Preserve that setup and explain the chosen population. An inner join would discard the invalid-reference rows that the orphan exercise needs to report; adding DISTINCT unnecessarily can also conceal separate employee identities that require individual attention.

## Verification needs both meaning and enforcement

Native reference-enforcement checks should exercise valid child insertion, invalid insertion and update, relevant parent changes, and any configured actions. They require a supported isolated schema and appropriate engine. Temporary query mirrors without foreign keys verify result semantics only. Keep those results distinct from exact MySQL/provider execution, applied application migrations, and authorization evidence.

A valid reference can remain valid across many child rows; foreign references need not be unique in the child relation. Also understand the source snapshot before diagnosing a live violation from exported data. Separately timed copies of parent and child relations can produce an inconsistent combined export that never existed as one live state. A trustworthy referential-integrity explanation identifies the relationship, optionality, relevant transitions, and actual evidence. It preserves the difference between an allowed absence, a current dangling proposal, and a real enforced write boundary.

questions.question_text: What does referential integrity guarantee?
options: That every column has a default value
A declared reference satisfies the defined parent-key relationship, with absence allowed only under its actual policy
That every table has a foreign key
That primary keys are always integers
questions.explanation: Optional single-column absence and composite missing-component behaviour must follow the actual supported definition.

questions.question_text: Which SQL mechanism directly enforces referential integrity?
options: UNIQUE constraint
FOREIGN KEY constraint
CHECK constraint
DEFAULT clause
questions.explanation: The FOREIGN KEY constraint is SQL's implementation of the referential integrity rule.

questions.question_text: For an optional single-column department reference, which query finds nonmissing employee references with no real parent?
options: SELECT * FROM employees WHERE department_id IS NOT NULL
SELECT e.* FROM employees e LEFT JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.department_id WHERE e.department_id IS NOT NULL AND d.id IS NULL
SELECT * FROM departments WHERE id IS NULL
SELECT * FROM employees INNER JOIN departments ON employees.department_id = departments.id
questions.explanation: A permitted NULL child reference is not an orphan. The parent identity supplies the match test.

questions.question_text: Does referential integrity guarantee that a foreign key reference is semantically correct, not just that it exists?
options: Yes, it guarantees full semantic correctness
No — it only guarantees the referenced row exists, not that it's the 'right' one for the business situation
It guarantees correctness only for numeric foreign keys
This distinction doesn't apply to referential integrity
questions.explanation: Referential integrity is purely about existence of the reference, not about whether it makes business sense.

questions.question_text: In real systems, why is referential integrity sometimes violated despite the concept being well understood?
options: It's impossible for this to happen in any real system
A FOREIGN KEY constraint may never have actually been declared, letting invalid references accumulate silently over time
Referential integrity is disabled by default in every SQL engine
SQL databases automatically ignore referential integrity after 1 million rows
questions.explanation: Without an actual enforced constraint, the relationship exists only by convention, and violations can silently accumulate.

questions.question_text: What operation on a parent row does referential integrity most directly restrict?
options: SELECT queries on the parent table
Deleting or updating a parent row that child rows still reference
Creating new columns on the parent table
Renaming the parent table
questions.explanation: Parent deletions and identifying updates must respect the configured supported restrictions or referential actions.

questions.question_text: What is the relationship between referential integrity and the foreign key constraint?
options: They are unrelated
Referential integrity is the conceptual/relational-model rule; FOREIGN KEY is the concrete SQL mechanism that enforces it
FOREIGN KEY is a stricter, unrelated concept
Referential integrity only applies to composite keys
questions.explanation: This mirrors the pattern of entity integrity/PRIMARY KEY — a theoretical rule paired with its concrete SQL enforcement mechanism.

questions.question_text: If department_id is NULL for an employee row, does this violate referential integrity?
options: Yes, always
No — NULL is a valid state (no reference yet) as long as the column allows it; only a non-NULL value pointing at a non-existent row would violate it
Only if department_id is also the primary key
This cannot be determined without more information about NULL handling in general
questions.explanation: A NULL foreign key simply means 'not referencing anything yet,' which is compatible with referential integrity, not a violation of it.

questions.question_text: Does an existing parent prove a reference is the correct business choice?
options: Yes; all existing choices are authorized
No; existence and semantic correctness differ
Only when numeric
Only if a name repeats
questions.explanation: Business eligibility and authority require separate checks.

questions.question_text: Why does an orphan audit exclude permitted NULL child references?
options: NULL always identifies parent zero
All nullable columns are invalid
They express optional absence rather than a dangling ordinary identity
LEFT JOIN cannot process NULL
questions.explanation: The audit must match the relationship’s absence policy.

questions.question_text: What can change a valid child into an invalid reference?
options: Renaming a query alias
Sorting by child id
Updating its reference to an absent parent identity
Selecting only one description
questions.explanation: Both INSERT and UPDATE paths can affect the invariant.

questions.question_text: Which parent attribute is suitable for an unmatched-parent test?
options: An optional descriptive label
The child’s display name
The source file name
A guaranteed non-NULL identifying key
questions.explanation: A missing optional description does not establish missing parent identity.

questions.question_text: Does a child primary key guarantee its parent references exist?
options: No; local identity and reference existence are separate
Yes; every primary key searches all parents
Only if composite
Only if positive
questions.explanation: Different constraints protect different invariants.

questions.question_text: Why might an export show a child lacking a parent despite enforced live constraints?
options: Every foreign key is advisory
Related tables may have been copied at inconsistent times
Exports always delete parents
Parent keys cannot be integers
questions.explanation: The combined export may not represent a consistent live state.

questions.question_text: Does an inner join suit an audit meant to list unmatched children?
options: Yes; it always preserves orphans
Only if ordered
No; it discards the unmatched facts the audit needs
Only if DISTINCT is added
questions.explanation: A preserving join or suitable anti-existence test is needed.

questions.question_text: What does NOT EXISTS ask in an orphan query?
options: Whether the child has no columns
Whether every department name repeats
Whether a primary key was generated
Whether no allowed parent matches the child’s reference
questions.explanation: It expresses an existence condition over the defined relationship.

questions.question_text: What does a grouped missing-parent count imply about automatic parent creation?
options: Nothing by itself; correction needs the domain’s authorized process
Every missing id must be inserted automatically
All parent labels should be guessed
The audit grants creation permission
questions.explanation: Diagnosis does not select a correction policy.

questions.question_text: Why assess composite references using their actual attributes?
options: All composites behave identically in every engine
Partial or mismatched components can name the wrong identity
Only the first component matters
Each component must be an independent parent row
questions.explanation: The whole intended reference must align with the parent identity.

questions.question_text: What can a temporary table mirror without foreign keys establish?
options: Native reference rejection
Production cascade behaviour
Query semantics on the supplied cases
Every provider’s engine configuration
questions.explanation: The fixture does not contain an enforcing FK boundary.

questions.question_text: Why avoid deleting a retired course automatically without reviewing history?
options: Referential integrity always demands history deletion
Every parent status is a foreign key
An audit authorizes all deletions
Historical enrollments may need the preserved parent identity
questions.explanation: Lifecycle and retention policy determine the appropriate transition.

coding_problems.title: Count nonmissing references that lack a department
coding_problems.task: Return one row invalid_references counting employees with non-NULL department_id and no matching department. NULL is permitted as unassigned.
coding_problems.seed_sql:
INSERT INTO departments (id, name) VALUES
(1, 'Engineering'),
(2, 'Sales'),
(3, 'Marketing');

INSERT INTO employees (id, name, email, department_id) VALUES
(1, 'Asha', 'asha@co.com', 1),
(2, 'Rohan', 'rohan@co.com', 1),
(3, 'Neha', 'neha@co.com', 2),
(4, 'Vikram', 'asha@co.com', 2),
(5, 'Priya', 'priya@co.com', 99),
(6, 'Karan', 'karan@co.com', 3),
(7, 'Divya', 'karan@co.com', 3),
(8, 'Aman', 'aman@co.com', 88);
constraints: Temporary mirrors deliberately omit foreign keys.
This audit checks reference existence only, not email uniqueness.
edge_cases: Unassigned employees are not invalid under the stated policy.
An empty employee population produces a zero count.
hints: Filter absence separately from unmatched nonmissing references.
A NOT EXISTS condition can test parent existence directly.
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS invalid_references FROM employees e WHERE e.department_id IS NOT NULL AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM departments d WHERE d.id = e.department_id);
coding_problems.explanation: The count follows optional single-column reference policy without asserting that an actual FK was executed.
